newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX heating oil ends sharply higher on API data.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX heating oil ends sharply higher on API data.

text.p: NYMEX heating oil prices ended sharply higher Wednesday after the American Petroleum Institute (API) reported a much smaller-than-expected build in distillate inventories.
October heating oil settled up 2.28 cents to 67.87 cents a gallon after rising as high as 68.00 cents a gallon.
October crude oil closed up 58 cents to $23.89 a barrel while October gasoline closed up 0.32 cent to 63.06 cents a gallon.
"The heating oil rally was spelled A-P-I," said Tim Evans, an analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group.
"It's a very tight inventory situation," said a trader.

On Tuesday, the API said total distillate stocks, of which heating oil is a component, grew a paltry 235,000 barrels for the week ended September 13, when traders had been expecting around a two million-barrel build to prepare for the winter.
Heating oil stocks are 20.7 million barrels below a year ago, and most of the shortfall is in the northeastern United States, the largest market in the world for heating oil.

Heating oil is also in tight supply in Europe. Analysts said U.S. exports of heating oil has increased while imports have decreased, signalling a possible competition between Europe and United States for supply.
Gas oil, the equivalent of heating oil in Europe, for October delivery rose $4.00 to $218.50 a tonne Wednesday on London's International Petroleum Exchange.
Meanwhile, crude oil followed heating oil upward, though a report of Iraqi shelling of Kurdish refugees also bolstered prices.
The official Iranian news agency said four Kurdish refugees were killed after the Iraqi army and the Kurdistan Democratic Party, a Kurdish faction, shelled a refugee camp in the Iranian border.
The report came amid the departure Wednesday of the first of the 3,500 U.S. ground troops to oil-rich Kuwait to defend the region following the latest tensions between the United States and Iraq.
Wednesday's rise in crude followed heavy selling days earlier, but Pegasus Econometric's Evans said those who remain invested in crude are longer-term believers in its bullish fundamentals.
"The speculative longs were flushed out during the sell-off, so the long positions are in more solid hands, and its going to take a lot to spook them," Evans said.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
